newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Lubumbashi wonders what's keeping Zaire rebels.
newsitem.headline: Lubumbashi wonders what's keeping Zaire rebels.

text.p: Residents of Zaire's second largest city Lubumbashi grew anxious on Tuesday as the sun rose with still no sign of an eagerly awaited rebel march into the key copper-mining centre.

"We have been waiting all night. We did not go home and we have not slept. We are waiting for Kabila," said Tshitshi Kasongo, a student standing by the road leading to a new southern front line that the rebels opened suddenly on Monday.
The hard core of Zairean soldiers blocking the path of Laurent Kabila's forces, who were believed to be only some 15 km (nine miles) away, said they were firmly in control.
"We have repulsed the enemy," said one member of the DSP, the special presidential guards who are the only part of the army which seems ready to put up a fight.
"The enemy has fled," said another who manned a checkpoint some five km (three miles) out of town towards the front line.

A dozen DSP soldiers were blocking the road. In front were their rebel foes, unseen, and just behind them were growing crowds of townspeople, unanimous in their support for Kabila and who begged for information on why the rebels had not come.
"The DSP must cede their positions and let them in. We don't want to die here," said Jean-Paul Banza, a 32-year-old farming scientist who lives nearby.

Lubumbashi's top general, Mokamba Bin Lowa, said on local radio on Monday that the situation was in hand and that his troops were blocking some 200 rebels who he said had crossed from Zambia in trucks provided by its government.
"We cannot surrender, we will attack and we will be victorious," he said.
One colonel told local businessmen on Monday that the rebels had been encircled in a surprise attack in a valley and that many had been killed.
It was impossible to verify the claim, but the thuds of mortars and rockets could be heard late on Monday several km (miles) south of Lubumbashi, and again on Tuesday morning.

Residents of the capital of Zaire's copper-mining heartland said they had also heard gunfire or detonations in the middle of the night from the direction of the airport, a 10-minute drive to the northeast.

The rebels had been closing in from the northwest and the northeast but were still believed to be some 200 km (125 miles) away before appearing from nowhere on Monday to take Kipushi, 30 km (18 miles) away on the Zambian border south of Lubumbashi.
State radio in Lusaka reported that Zambian commandos had been sent to the Zaire border area adjoining Lubumbashi.

"A contingent of Zambian commandos are said to have been deployed along the border between Kipushi and Kasumbalesa border post following the fall of Kipushi to Zairean rebels," the radio said, adding that business at the border crossing was normal.
Some people suspect that the rebel attack on Kipushi was a ploy to lure the city's defenders out in one direction and to then push in from another.
At least one brigade of Lubumbashi's soldiers changed sides on Monday as the rebel arrival looked imminent.
They donned white headbands -- a sign of support for Kabila's alliance -- and decked their barracks out with white flags made from maize meal sacks.
No one outside the military is sure how many DSP soldiers are in Lubumbashi or how strong is their will to fight.
The army lost Zaire's third largest city Kisangani in the northern jungle last month without a fight, despite reinforcing it heavily after the government vowed to defend it.
No such pledge has been made for Lubumbashi, 1,800 km (1,100 miles) away from the capital Kinshasa in Shaba province which has long struggled for independence.
